newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu asks Palestinians not to lose faith.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu asks Palestinians not to lose faith.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday appealed to Palestinians not to lose hope in peace talks and said a Washington summit Palestinians called a failure was a chance for a "fresh start" on peace.

"I ask you, don't go into mourning. Don't lose hope," Netanyahu said on Israel Channel One television's Arabic service in an address to Palestinians. "This is an opportunity for a fresh start for the peace process," Netanyahu said.
Netanyahu appealed to Palestinians to remain calm and have faith in negotiations scheduled to resume on Sunday at Erez checkpoint on the border between Israel and self-ruled Gaza.

"I want to say something to Palestinian viewers. There are no winners and no losers if we fight each other," Netanyahu said. "If we fight each other and if we return to bloody riots, we will both be losers. If we walk together on the process of peace...we will both be winners," Netanyahu said.
Netanyahu returned on Thursday from a White House crisis summit, hailed as a success by Israel, called after a week of violence.

Palestinians called the summit a failure after Palestinian President Yasser Arafat failed to win a target date for a long-delayed Israeli troop pullback in the West Bank town of Hebron or an Israeli pledge to close a Jerusalem tunnel whose opening last week sparked clashes which killed more than 70.
Netanyahu said Israel and the Palestinians were still far from a solution to their problems but that progress could be achieved in accelerated negotiations starting on Sunday.

"There is a way to move forward and this is around the negotiating table," Netanyahu said. He said the Erez talks would focus on security issues and the Hebron redeployment, agreed to by Israel's previous government.
Netanyahu said he intended to honour the Hebron deal "with proper security arrangements, of course." Palestinians have rejected any renegotiation of the plan.

The tone of Netanyahu's appeal stood in marked contrast to comments before the Washington summit in which the prime minister accused Arafat of having incited last week's violence -- the worst Israeli-Palestinian bloodshed since a 1993 peace deal.
In Morocco, Arafat said the future of Middle East peace depended on Israel's next move.

"It depends how the Israelis will deal. Especially we are insisting they implement accurately and honestly what has been agreed upon and what was signed," Arafat said after talks with Moroccan King Hassan.
A senior Israeli official who returned with Netanyahu from the summit said on Thursday Israelis and Palestinians needed a "stabilisation period" of a few months after the explosion of violence.
"(This is) so the two military structures can gain confidence to work together," said the official, who spoke on condition he not be named.

Israeli defence officials were due to discuss soon with Netanyahu what to do about Israeli tanks in the West Bank, Israeli officials said. They said Israel might ease the siege that bars Palestinian travel between autonomous cities, if calm prevailed.
